All data-analysis and survey-design scripts, sufficient to reproduce the analyses reported here, are available in the project's [GitHub repository](https://github.com/datsimon-design/Masters_Project).

## Survey design
This study was originally planned as a vessel-based line-transect survey. Logistical constraints prevented deployment of the survey vessel within the field-season window, and the survey was consequently redesigned as a land-based point-transect survey conducted from three fixed vantage points (see Supplemental Material for the original design and the constraints encountered).

Observations were made from three vantage points selected to sample the eastern, southern, and western sectors of the BGTW: Sandy Bay (East), Europa Point (South) and Prince George (West) (@fig-overview, @tbl-landspots). Together these covered parts of the territory, and estimates therefore apply to the surveyed sectors rather than to the BGTW as a whole (@fig-spots).

Surveys were conducted between 08 May 2026 and 07 July 2026. Each watch consisted of 10 minutes on-effort followed by a 20-minute break, allowing observers to rest and reducing the likelihood of double-counting by permitting animals to leave the surveyed area [@gutierrez-munozPatternsTrendsCetacean2021]. Watches were postponed when visibility was poor or sea state exceeded Beaufort 5.

Observations were made with the naked eye and with binoculars (Fujinon 7 × 50) using a continuous horizon scanning method [@mannBehavioralSamplingMethods1999]. For each sighting, the time, number of vertical reticles, horizontal bearing, species, group size, and behavioural state were recorded, together with the presence of birds or fish where possible. Behavioural states followed an adaptation of Neumann et al. [-@neumannBehaviourEcologyCommon] and Hawkins and Gartside [-@hawkinsInteractiveBehavioursBottlenose2009] (Travelling, Milling, Foraging, Socialising, and Resting) (see **Table S5**). Photographs were taken opportunistically (Canon EOS R50 with a 100–400 mm telephoto lens) to support subsequent species confirmation (see Supplemental for detailed information).

![Views from the three vantage points, Prince George (A), Sandy Bay (B), and Europa Point (C), facing left (a), right (b), and a wide shot of each station (c). Panel D shows the area covered by each station's scan sector.](/figures/spots_comb.png){#fig-spots}

## Data Analysis
### Distance calculation{#sec-calc}
Radial distance to each sighting from the observation point ($d$) was derived from reticle readings following the shore-based principle of Lerczak and Hobbs [-@lerczakCalculatingSightingDistances1998], adapted here to account for sea-surface curvature and, at the western station, for a coastline reference. The depression angle to a target at horizontal distance $d$ was modelled as

$$
\theta = \frac{h}{d} + \frac{d}{2R}
$$

where $h$ is the observer eye height above sea level and $R$ the Earth's radius (6,371 km); the second term corrects for the curvature of the sea surface between observer and target. The total depression angle to a sighting is the angle of the reference line ($\theta_{ref}$) plus the reticle angle,

$$
\theta = \theta_{ref} + r\times F,
$$

where $r$ is the number of reticles subtended between the sighting and the reference line and $F$ the binocular-specific reticle factor (0.005 for the Fujinon 7 × 50 FMTRC-SX binoculars used here). Distance was then recovered by inverting the quadratic:

$$
d = R\times\theta - \sqrt{(R\times\theta)^2 - 2R\times h}.
$$

At the open-water stations (Europa Point, Sandy Bay), the reference line was the sea horizon, for which $\theta_{ref} = \sqrt{2h/R}$. Combined with the horizontal bearing, each distance was used to project the sighting location from the observer's position for mapping (see Appendix D).

Because of the enclosed nature of the western survey area (the Bay of Gibraltar), the far shore rather than the sea horizon was visible along most bearings from the Prince George station. The coastline sits closer than the true horizon and therefore at a greater angle of depression, so applying the horizon reference would overestimate sighting distances. For this station the reference distance ($d_{ref}$) was instead determined per bearing: using a detailed polygon of the bay's coastline (including the detached mole off Algeciras, the first visible obstacle on some bearings), a ray was cast from the observation point along the recorded horizontal bearing, and the distance to the first intersection with land was taken as $d_{ref}$. The reference depression angle was then $\theta_{ref} = h/d_{ref} + d_{ref}/(2R)$, entering the same total-angle expression and inversion above. Bearings pointing out of the bay mouth, where no coastline was intersected, reverted to the horizon reference. Worked examples in R are provided in the Supplementary Material and the project repository ([GitHub](https://github.com/datsimon-design/Masters_Project)).

### Kernel Density Estimation (KDE)
Kernel density estimation (KDE) is a well-established tool for describing the spatial distribution and relative abundance of cetaceans [@raymentKernelDensityEstimates2009; @milmannTemporalSpatialDistribution2017]. It was used here to describe the relative spatial distribution of cetaceans within the BGTW. The locations of all on-effort sightings—derived from reticle-based radial distances and compass bearings (see @sec-calc), were projected to UTM zone 30N so that smoothing was performed in metric units, and used as input to the kernel density estimation. A bivariate kernel density surface was computed in R using the `ks` package [@duongKsKernelSmoothing2005], with each sighting weighted by its group size so that the surface reflected the relative density of individuals rather than of sightings alone. The smoothing bandwidth was selected automatically using a plug-in bandwidth matrix [@duongPluginBandwidthMatrices2003], and density was evaluated over a 100 × 100 grid spanning the survey area.

Because the resulting surface is a normalised probability density (integrating to one), it provides a descriptive, relative measure of spatial concentration; it was not corrected for observation effort or imperfect detection, which were instead accounted for separately through the distance-sampling density estimation (@sec-det_func). The surface was visualised over the study area and overlaid with the observation stations and individual sightings to identify areas of elevated cetacean occurrence.

### Detection Function {#sec-det_func}
The `Distance` package [@marshallDistanceDistanceSampling2025] requires a flatfile format [@bucklandDistanceSamplingMethods2015] (see Appendix F); the data from the effort and sighting logs were therefore first mutated and then joined, the effort was calculated by dividing the sector degrees by 360. The area for each wedge was calculated and added to the data frame. The truncation distance was determined separately for each sampling location based on the corresponding distribution of observed distances (Europa Point = 4,500 m; Sandy Bay = 12,000 m; Prince George = 8,000 m). Detection functions were first fitted per station using the `ds` function, following a two-step procedure: candidate key functions (half-normal and hazard-rate) were compared by AIC, goodness-of-fit test (`gof_ds`), and Q–Q plot, and the best-supported key function was then tested with candidate covariates (wave height, glare, sea state, and wind speed) to assess whether they improved fit. 

Because the per-station samples were insufficient to support stable detection functions [@bucklandDistanceSamplingMethods2015], a single pooled detection function was additionally fitted across all stations, following the same two-step procedure; for the pooled model, observation height was tested as an additional covariate alongside those above. The pooled detection function was used for the density estimates reported here, with per-station estimates retained for comparison. Density was estimated separately for groups and individuals.

### Statistical Analysis
All statistical analyses were carried out in R [@zotero-item-2907]. Sightings per unit effort (SPUE), calculated as the number of sightings per on-effort scan, was strongly right-skewed and zero-inflated and did not meet the assumptions of parametric analysis of variance (normality of residuals and homogeneity of variance). A non-parametric approach was therefore adopted, with each on-effort scan treated as the sampling unit. Differences in SPUE among the three active observation stations (Europa Point, Sandy Bay and Prince George) were tested using a Kruskal–Wallis rank-sum test [@KruskalWallis1952]. Where the omnibus test was significant, pairwise differences were identified using Dunn's post-hoc test [@dunnMultipleComparisonsUsing1964]. Dunn's test operates on the pooled ranks of the Kruskal–Wallis test and accounts appropriately for tied values. P-values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate procedure [@benjaminiControllingFalseDiscovery1995].


### Comparison with opportunistic records
To evaluate the systematic survey against existing opportunistic data, occurrence records of *Delphinus delphis* were retrieved from the OBIS ([OBIS Mapper](https://mapper.obis.org/), accessed 30 July 2026) using the `robis` package [@provoostRobisOceanBiodiversity2022], constrained to a bounding box encompassing the study area (Latitude: -5.438 to -5.248, Longitude: 36.05 to 36.195). Records lacking coordinates were excluded, and the remainder were projected to WGS 84 and assigned to survey sectors by spatial intersection with the stratum polygons. The spatial distribution of opportunistic records was then compared with that of the systematic on-effort sightings, both visually and by tabulating record counts per sector. Because opportunistic records carry no associated survey effort, the comparison was restricted to spatial coverage and was not interpreted in terms of relative abundance.
